items.quote: Rated capacity means the maximum working load permitted by the manufacturer under specified working conditions. Such working conditions typically include a specific combination of factors such as equipment configuration, radii, boom length, and other parameters of use.

items.definition: When operating on a short cycle operation, refers to the rope being used on a single layer and spooled repeatedly over a short portion of the drum.
items.quote: Repetitive pickup points refer to, when operating on a short cycle operation, the rope being used on a single layer and being spooled repetitively over a short portion of the drum.

items.definition: A wire rope that moves over sheaves or drums.
items.quote: Running wire rope means a wire rope that moves over sheaves or drums.

items.definition: A firm, level surface designed, prepared and designated as a travel path for the weight and configuration of the crane used to lift and travel with the crane suspended platform. An existing surface may be used if it meets these criteria.
items.quote: Runway means a firm, level surface designed, prepared and designated as a path of travel for the weight and configuration of the crane being used to lift and travel with the crane suspended platform. An existing surface may be used as long as it meets these criteria.

items.definition: A section of this subpart, unless otherwise specified.
items.quote: Section means a section of this subpart, unless otherwise specified.

items.definition: A track-type or wheel-type tractor with a side-mounted boom, used to lift, lower or transport a load suspended on the load hook. The boom or hook can be lifted or lowered only vertically.
items.quote: Sideboom crane means a track-type or wheel-type tractor having a boom mounted on the side of the tractor, used for lifting, lowering or transporting a load suspended on the load hook. The boom or hook can be lifted or lowered in a vertical direction only.

items.definition: Warnings of site-specific hazards, such as proximity of power lines.
items.quote: Special hazard warnings means warnings of site-specific hazards (for example, proximity of power lines).

items.definition: The tendency of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other flotation means to return upright after being inclined by an external force.
items.quote: Stability (flotation device) means the tendency of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation to return to an upright position after having been inclined by an external force.

items.definition: The protocol for hand signals in appendix A of this subpart.
items.quote: Standard Method means the protocol in appendix A of this subpart for hand signals.

items.definition: Means "such as, but not limited to."
items.quote: Such as means “such as, but not limited to.”

items.definition: A rope, usually fiber, attached to a lifted load to control load spinning and pendular motions, or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling.
items.quote: Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations.

items.definition: An individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver.
items.quote: Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver.

items.definition: Raising or lowering a load from horizontal to vertical or from vertical to horizontal.
items.quote: Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal.
items.term: Tilt up or tilt down operation

items.definition: A lifting structure using a vertical mast or tower to support an elevated working boom (jib) that carries suspended loads; the boom may be fixed (horizontal or angled) or luffing but can always rotate to swing loads by top slewing or bottom slewing, and the base may be fixed or ballasted and moveable. Mobile cranes configured with luffing jib and/or tower attachments are not considered tower cranes under this section.
items.quote: Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position. Loads are suspended from the working boom. While the working boom may be of the fixed type (horizontal or angled) or have luffing capability, it can always rotate to swing loads, either by rotating on the top of the tower (top slewing) or by the rotation of the tower (bottom slewing). The tower base may be fixed in one location or ballasted and moveable between locations. Mobile cranes that are configured with luffing jib and/or tower attachments are not considered tower cranes under this section.

items.definition: For tower cranes, an assembly of two or more axles arranged to allow vertical wheel displacement and equalize loading on the wheels.
items.quote: Travel bogie (tower cranes) is an assembly of two or more axles arranged to permit vertical wheel displacement and equalize the loading on the wheels.

items.definition: The angle of inclination about the transverse axis of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other flotation means.
items.quote: Trim means angle of inclination about the transverse axis of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of floatation.

items.definition: A condition in which the uppermost component on the hoist line, such as the load block, hook block, overhaul ball or similar, contacts the boom tip, fixed upper block or similar component. This binds the system, and continued power can cause the hoist rope or another component to fail.
items.quote: Two blocking means a condition in which a component that is uppermost on the hoist line such as the load block, hook block, overhaul ball, or similar component, comes in contact with the boom tip, fixed upper block or similar component. This binds the system and continued application of power can cause failure of the hoist rope or other component.

items.definition: Procedures that are no longer available from the manufacturer or have never been available from the manufacturer.
items.quote: Unavailable procedures means procedures that are no longer available from the manufacturer, or have never been available, from the manufacturer.

items.definition: Means "up to and including."
items.quote: Up to means “up to and including.”

items.definition: The revolving frame of equipment on which the operating machinery (and in many cases the engine) are mounted along with the operator's cab. The counterweight is typically supported at the rear of the upperstructure, and the boom or other front end attachment is mounted at the front.
items.quote: Upperworks means the revolving frame of equipment on which the operating machinery (and many cases the engine) are mounted along with the operator's cab. The counterweight is typically supported on the rear of the upperstructure and the boom or other front end attachment is mounted on the front.

items.definition: A flexible rope made by laying steel wires into various patterns of multi-wired strands around a core system to produce a helically wound rope.
items.quote: Wire rope means a flexible rope constructed by laying steel wires into various patterns of multi-wired strands around a core system to produce a helically wound rope.

items.definition: The ability of the ground to support the equipment, including slope, compaction, and firmness.
items.quote: “Ground conditions” means the ability of the ground to support the equipment (including slope, compaction, and firmness).

items.definition: Blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies (in marshes/wetlands), or similar supporting materials or devices.
items.quote: “Supporting materials” means blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies (in marshes/wetlands), or similar supporting materials or devices.

items.definition: The person who directs assembly/disassembly, which must be either someone who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons. If only one person performs the assembly/disassembly, that person must meet both sets of criteria and is considered the A/D director for purposes of this standard.
items.quote:
Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (“A/D director”).
(2) Where the assembly/disassembly is being performed by only one person, that person must meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. For purposes of this standard, that person is considered the A/D director.

items.definition: An aid the dedicated spotter must be equipped with to help identify the minimum clearance distance. Examples include, but are not limited to, a clearly visible line painted on the ground, a clearly visible line of stanchions, or a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the spotter and a building corner ahead of the spotter).
items.quote: (A) Be equipped with a visual aid to assist in identifying the minimum clearance distance. Examples of a visual aid include, but are not limited to: A clearly visible line painted on the ground; a clearly visible line of stanchions; a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the dedicated spotter and a building corner ahead of the dedicated spotter).

items.definition: The employer identifies it in one of two ways. One is to demarcate boundaries (such as with flags, a range limit device or a range control warning device) and prohibit the operator from operating the equipment past them. The other is to define it as the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius.
items.quote:
(1) Identify the work zone by either:
(i) Demarcating boundaries (such as with flags, or a device such as a range limit device or range control warning device) and prohibiting the operator from operating the equipment past those boundaries, or
(ii) Defining the work zone as the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius.

items.definition: An aid to help identify the minimum clearance distance. Examples include, but are not limited to, a clearly visible line painted on the ground, a clearly visible line of stanchions, or a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the dedicated spotter and a building corner ahead of the spotter).
items.quote: (A) Be equipped with a visual aid to assist in identifying the minimum clearance distance. Examples of a visual aid include, but are not limited to: A clearly visible line painted on the ground; a clearly visible line of stanchions; a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the dedicated spotter and a building corner ahead of the dedicated spotter).

items.definition: A term the text attaches to the danger of the potentially energized zone around the equipment.
items.quote: (D) The danger of the potentially energized zone around the equipment (step potential).

items.definition: An aid the dedicated spotter must be equipped with to help identify the minimum clearance distance. Examples include, but are not limited to, a line painted on the ground, a clearly visible line of stanchions, or a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks, such as a fence post behind the spotter and a building corner ahead of the spotter.
items.quote: (i) Be equipped with a visual aid to assist in identifying the minimum clearance distance. Examples of a visual aid include, but are not limited to: A line painted on the ground; a clearly visible line of stanchions; a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the dedicated spotter and a building corner ahead of the dedicated spotter).

items.definition: A category of apparent wire rope deficiencies that includes significant distortion of the rope structure (such as kinking, crushing, unstranding, birdcaging, signs of core failure or steel core protrusion between the outer strands) and significant corrosion. It also includes electric arc damage from a source other than power lines or heat damage, improperly applied end connections, and significantly corroded, cracked, bent, or worn end connections (such as from severe service).
items.quote:
Category I. Apparent deficiencies in this category include the following:
(A) Significant distortion of the wire rope structure such as kinking, crushing, unstranding, birdcaging, signs of core failure or steel core protrusion between the outer strands.
(B) Significant corrosion.
(C) Electric arc damage (from a source other than power lines) or heat damage.
(D) Improperly applied end connections.
(E) Significantly corroded, cracked, bent, or worn end connections (such as from severe service).

items.definition: A category of apparent wire rope deficiencies made up of visible broken wires and a diameter reduction of more than 5% from nominal diameter. The broken wire levels for running ropes are six randomly distributed in one rope lay or three in one strand in one rope lay, where a rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around it. For rotation resistant ropes, they are two randomly distributed in six rope diameters or four randomly distributed in 30 rope diameters. For pendants or standing ropes, they are more than two in one rope lay in rope beyond end connections and/or more than one in a rope lay at an end connection.
items.quote:
Category II. Apparent deficiencies in this category are:
(A) Visible broken wires, as follows:
(1) In running wire ropes: Six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay, where a rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around the rope.
(2) In rotation resistant ropes: Two randomly distributed broken wires in six rope diameters or four randomly distributed broken wires in 30 rope diameters.
(3) In pendants or standing wire ropes: More than two broken wires in one rope lay located in rope beyond end connections and/or more than one broken wire in a rope lay located at an end connection.
(B) A diameter reduction of more than 5% from nominal diameter.

items.definition: The length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around the rope.
items.quote: In running wire ropes: Six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay, where a rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around the rope.

items.definition: A category of apparent wire rope deficiencies that includes core protrusion or other distortion indicating core failure in rotation resistant wire rope, prior electrical contact with a power line, and a broken strand.
items.quote:
Category III. Apparent deficiencies in this category include the following:
(A) In rotation resistant wire rope, core protrusion or other distortion indicating core failure.
(B) Prior electrical contact with a power line.
(C) A broken strand.

items.definition: Items that the competent person must give particular attention to: rotation resistant wire rope in use; rope used for boom hoists and luffing hoists, particularly at reverse bends; and rope at flange points, crossover points and repetitive pickup points on drums. They also include rope at or near terminal ends, and rope in contact with saddles, equalizer sheaves or other sheaves where rope travel is limited.
items.quote:
Critical review items. The competent person must give particular attention to all of the following:
(i) Rotation resistant wire rope in use.
(ii) Wire rope being used for boom hoists and luffing hoists, particularly at reverse bends.
(iii) Wire rope at flange points, crossover points and repetitive pickup points on drums.
(iv) Wire rope at or near terminal ends.
(v) Wire rope in contact with saddles, equalizer sheaves or other sheaves where rope travel is limited.

items.definition: Also called "Type I", this is stranded rope built to have little or no tendency to rotate or, if guided, to transmit little or no torque. It has at least 15 outer strands in an assembly of at least three layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations, with the outer strands laid in the opposite direction to the underlying layer.
items.quote: Type I rotation resistant wire rope (“Type I”). Type I rotation resistant rope is stranded rope constructed to have little or no tendency to rotate or, if guided, transmits little or no torque. It has at least 15 outer strands and comprises an assembly of at least three layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations. The direction of lay of the outer strands is opposite to that of the underlying layer.
items.term: Type I rotation resistant wire rope

items.definition: Also called "Type II", this is stranded rope built to have significant resistance to rotation. It has at least 10 outer strands in an assembly of two or more layers of strands laid helically over a center in two or three operations, with the outer strands laid in the opposite direction to the underlying layer.
items.quote: Type II rotation resistant wire rope (“Type II”). Type II rotation resistant rope is stranded rope constructed to have significant resistance to rotation. It has at least 10 outer strands and comprises an assembly of two or more layers of strands laid helically over a center in two or three operations. The direction of lay of the outer strands is opposite to that of the underlying layer.
items.term: Type II rotation resistant wire rope

items.definition: Also called "Type III", this is stranded rope built to have limited resistance to rotation. It has no more than nine outer strands in an assembly of two layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations, with the outer strands laid in the opposite direction to the underlying layer.
items.quote: Type III rotation resistant wire rope (“Type III”). Type III rotation resistant rope is stranded rope constructed to have limited resistance to rotation. It has no more than nine outer strands, and comprises an assembly of two layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations. The direction of lay of the outer strands is opposite to that of the underlying layer.
items.term: Type III rotation resistant wire rope

items.definition: For the ropes this provision covers, it must be the total minimum breaking force of all parts of rope in the system, divided by the load on the rope system when it supports the static weights of the structure and the load within the equipment's rated capacity.
items.quote: The operating design factor for these ropes must be the total minimum breaking force of all parts of rope in the system divided by the load imposed on the rope system when supporting the static weights of the structure and the load within the equipment's rated capacity.

items.definition: The load travel, or the area near or at load placement.
items.quote: The point of operation, meaning the load travel or the area near or at load placement, is not in full view of the operator.

items.definition: A term the text uses in connection with a boom that is designed to free fall.
items.quote: (1) The use of equipment in which the boom is designed to free fall (live boom) is prohibited in each of the following circumstances:

items.definition: A Federal employee of the Department of Defense or Armed Forces. Employees of private contractors are not included.
items.quote: An employee of the U.S. military is a Federal employee of the Department of Defense or Armed Forces and does not include employees of private contractors.

items.definition: The individual who must continuously monitor an operator-in-training while the trainee operates the equipment. This person must be an employee or agent of the trainee's employer and have the knowledge, training, and experience needed to direct the trainee on the equipment in use.
items.quote:
While operating the equipment, the operator-in-training must be continuously monitored by an individual (“operator's trainer”) who meets all of the following requirements:
[29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)(i)(A)] (A) The operator's trainer is an employee or agent of the operator-in-training's employer.
[29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)(i)(B)] (B) The operator's trainer has the knowledge, training, and experience necessary to direct the operator-in-training on the equipment in use.

items.definition: Size and configuration includes lifting capacity, boom length, attachments, luffing jib and counterweight set-up, but is not limited to these.
items.quote: Size and configuration includes, but is not limited to, lifting capacity, boom length, attachments, luffing jib, and counterweight set-up.

items.definition: A certification that is not portable meets the relevant certification requirements only where the operator is employed by, and operating the equipment for, the employer that issued it.
items.quote: Not portable: Such a certification meets the requirements of paragraph (c) of this section only where the operator is employed by (and operating the equipment for) the employer that issued the certification.

items.definition:
These are the things each signal person must meet:
- Know and understand the type of signals used, including the Standard Method for hand signals if hand signals are used.
- Be competent in applying that type of signals.
- Have a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including the crane dynamics involved in swinging and stopping loads and boom deflection from hoisting loads.
- Know and understand the relevant requirements of the cited rules.
- Demonstrate that they meet all of the above through an oral or written test, and through a practical test.
items.quote:
Qualification Requirements. Each signal person must:
(1) Know and understand the type of signals used. If hand signals are used, the signal person must know and understand the Standard Method for hand signals.
(2) Be competent in the application of the type of signals used.
(3) Have a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including the crane dynamics involved in swinging and stopping loads and boom deflection from hoisting loads.
(4) Know and understand the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428.
(5) Demonstrate that he/she meets the requirements in paragraphs (c)(1) through (4) of this section through an oral or written test, and through a practical test.

items.definition: An assessment by an employer's qualified evaluator under the employer's qualified evaluator option is not portable. This means other employers are not permitted to use it to meet the signal person qualification requirements.
items.quote: An assessment by an employer's qualified evaluator under this option is not portable—other employers are not permitted to use it to meet the requirements of this section.

items.definition: The devices listed in this section. They are required on all tower cranes covered by this subpart, unless otherwise specified.
items.quote: The devices listed in this section (“operational aids”) are required on all tower cranes covered by this subpart, unless otherwise specified.

items.definition: Powered equipment made up of a mast or equivalent member held at or near the end by guys or braces, with or without a boom, plus its hoisting mechanism. The hoisting mechanism (typically base-mounted) and operating ropes move the mast or equivalent member, the load, or both. Types include A-frame, basket, breast, Chicago boom, gin pole (except gin poles used to erect communication towers), guy, shearleg, stiffleg, and variations of such equipment.
items.quote: A derrick is powered equipment consisting of a mast or equivalent member that is held at or near the end by guys or braces, with or without a boom, and its hoisting mechanism. The mast/equivalent member and/or the load is moved by the hoisting mechanism (typically base-mounted) and operating ropes. Derricks include: A-frame, basket, breast, Chicago boom, gin pole (except gin poles used for erection of communication towers), guy, shearleg, stiffleg, and variations of such equipment.

items.definition: A collective term for barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation.
items.quote: This section contains supplemental requirements for floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation (i.e., vessel/flotation device).

items.definition: The vertical distance between the water line and the main deck of the vessel.
items.quote: Freeboard is the vertical distance between the water line and the main deck of the vessel.

items.definition: The crane/derrick is physically attached to the barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation. Methods include crossed-cable systems attached to the crane/derrick and vessel/flotation device; bolting, welding or chain-strapping the crane/derrick to the vessel/flotation device; or other methods of physical attachment.
items.quote: Option (1)—Physical attachment. The crane/derrick is physically attached to the barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation. Methods of physical attachment include crossed-cable systems attached to the crane/derrick and vessel/flotation device, bolting or welding the crane/derrick to the vessel/flotation device, strapping the crane/derrick to the vessel/flotation device with chains, or other methods of physical attachment.

items.definition: Preventing the crane/derrick from shifting by installing barricade restraints, also called a corralling system.
items.quote: Option (2)—Corralling. The crane/derrick is prevented from shifting by installing barricade restraints (i.e., a corralling system).

items.definition: An option in which the crane/derrick is prevented from shifting by being mounted to a wire rope system.
items.quote: Option (4)—Centerline cable system. The crane/derrick is prevented from shifting by being mounted to a wire rope system.

items.definition: The text equates rated capacities with working load limits. In the quoted rule for alloy steel-chain slings, these are indicated on the sling by permanently affixed, legible identification markings prescribed by the manufacturer, and employers must not use the slings with loads above them.
items.quote: Employers must not use alloy steel-chain slings with loads in excess of the rated capacities (i.e., working load limits) indicated on the sling by permanently affixed and legible identification markings prescribed by the manufacturer.

items.definition: Handling loads out of the operator's vision.
items.quote: Handling loads out of the operator's vision (“operating in the blind”).
